1.definition: Song dynasty general who commanded the garrison at Xiangyang during the Mongol siege of 1267–1273. He held the city for six years through encirclement and bombardment, the longest single-point defense of the entire Song-Mongol war. His eventual surrender in 1273 opened the Yangtze corridor to the Mongol advance southward.

Persian military engineer from the Ilkhanate who, with his colleague Ismail, was hired by Kublai Khan in 1271 to design counterweight trebuchets for the siege of Xiangyang. Their machines, called huihui pao ("Muslim machines") in Chinese sources, threw projectiles of roughly 220 pounds over 200 yards and broke through walls that conventional Song-era siege engines could not crack.

2.definition: The northernmost sections of the extended Grand Canal, built by Kublai Khan's engineers between 1293 and 1293, connecting the existing canal system directly to the new capital Khanbaliq (Beijing). The construction required roughly 200,000 conscripted laborers and solved the grain-supply problem of feeding a capital city far from the Yangtze agricultural heartland.

4.definition: Franciscan friar who served as a Catholic bishop in Central Asia and China in the mid-fourteenth century, one of several Catholic missionaries who followed John of Montecorvino's establishment of the archbishopric of Beijing. He wrote a letter from Almalic (in modern Kazakhstan) in 1338 describing the Mongol-era Catholic mission in Asia.

5.matchText: The Secret History of the Mongols

5.definition: Mongol-era poet (c. 1272–1340) who wrote in classical Chinese despite his Inner Asian Mongolian background — one of the rare Yuan-period writers who bridged the Mongol and Han literary traditions. His ci poetry (a song-lyric form with prescribed tonal patterns) was highly regarded by later Chinese critics as evidence that Yuan culture produced genuine Chinese literary achievements across ethnic lines.

Han Chinese scholar-officials and educated men who refused to serve the Yuan dynasty after the Song fell in 1279 — the yimin (literally "leftover people") who maintained loyalty to the defunct dynasty as a form of Confucian integrity. Many redirected their cultural energies into painting, calligraphy, and writing rather than government service, making the yimin tradition a major driver of Yuan-era literati art.

6.definition: The integrated postal-and-trade road system maintained across the Mongol khanates from the 1250s to the 1340s — relay stations stocked with horses and lodging every 25–30 miles, trade passports (paiza) that gave authorized merchants imperial protection, and caravan routes linking China to Persia to the Black Sea. This network made possible the large-scale movement of silk, porcelain, astronomical knowledge, and — inadvertently — the Yersinia pestis bacterium that caused the Black Death.

Kublai Khan's imperial bureau charged with astronomy, calendar reform, and mathematical sciences. It was staffed by both Chinese astronomers (notably Guo Shoujing) and Persian and Arab specialists (notably Jamal al-Din from the Maragha observatory), and produced the Shoushi calendar of 1281 — the most accurate astronomical calendar of the medieval world, calculating the tropical year at 365.2425 days, the same figure the Gregorian calendar would adopt three centuries later.

The Yuan dynasty astronomical calendar compiled by the Chinese astronomer Guo Shoujing in 1281, incorporating both Chinese and Islamic astronomical methods. It calculated the solar year at 365.2425 days — identical to the Gregorian calendar introduced in Europe three centuries later — and remained the official Chinese calendar for 363 years until the Qing dynasty replaced it.

The tradition of medicinal plant knowledge systematized in texts like the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica). Under the Yuan, Chinese pharmacological knowledge was compiled alongside Persian and Arab medical texts in the Huihui Yaofang (Muslim Pharmaceutical Formulas), a 36-volume synthesis prepared for the imperial library that remains one of the great cross-cultural medical texts of the pre-modern era.

7.definition: The Yuan dynasty's paper currency, issued empire-wide beginning with Kublai's Zhongtong notes in 1260 and expanded under the Zhiyuan reform of 1287. Backed at issue by silver and silk reserves and declared the sole legal tender for major transactions, jiaochao was the most extensive fiat currency system in pre-modern history. Chronic over-issuance from the 1310s onward eroded its value; by the 1340s the notes traded at deep discounts and by the 1350s they were effectively worthless in rural markets, destroying the dynasty's fiscal capacity precisely when it most needed funds to suppress rebellion.

8.definition: A small rural Buddhist monastery in Fengyang county, Anhui province, where the orphaned Zhu Yuanzhang took refuge after his family died in the famine of 1344. He became a novice monk there before being sent out to beg — the itinerant years that gave him his familiarity with the suffering of the Yuan peasantry and contact with White Lotus millenarian networks. The temple was later renamed Longxing Monastery and honored by the Ming court as the starting point of the dynasty's founding emperor.
